before: A worked approach to comparing forecasts and outcomes, using a synthetic dataset rather than measured estimator performance.
after: How to compare difficulty forecasts fairly, with a worked calculation using made-up values. The example does not measure any forecaster’s performance.
note: States the question and synthetic limitation directly; no measured-performance claim.

before: Compare the same question
after: Match the target and forecast time
note: Names the section’s question or concrete subject. Section key and ID stay unchanged.

before: A fair comparison starts with the same target block, difficulty-change definition and forecast time. Comparing a forecast issued early in the adjustment period with a later one gives the later forecast information the earlier one did not have.
after: A fair comparison asks each forecast the same question: what will the difficulty change be at the same target block? Use the same definition of difficulty change and compare forecasts issued at the same time. A later forecast has information that an earlier one did not.
note: Preserves same target, definition, timing, information advantage, original records, provenance fields and treatment of failures or missing forecasts.

before: Record the forecast as it was issued, the input block height, source, model version and outcome definition. Preserve failed and missing forecasts in the evaluation record rather than selecting only successful predictions.
after: Keep each forecast as originally issued, together with its input block height, source, model version and definition of the outcome. Include failed and missing forecasts in the record. Selecting only successful predictions would change the comparison.
note: Preserves same target, definition, timing, information advantage, original records, provenance fields and treatment of failures or missing forecasts.

before: Measure error and uncertainty separately
after: Error and forecast ranges
note: Names the section’s question or concrete subject. Section key and ID stay unchanged.

before: Absolute error is the distance between a forecast and its outcome. Mean absolute error averages that distance over the selected observations. It describes that evaluation set; it does not establish how a model will perform in another period.
after: Absolute error is the size of the gap between a forecast and its outcome. Mean absolute error averages those gaps across the forecasts being tested. It describes that sample, not how the model will perform in another period.
note: Retains error definition, sample limit, coverage versus width and calibration requirements; explains calibration rather than leaving jargon unexplained.

before: An interval needs a separate check: how often did outcomes fall inside the stated range, and how wide was it? Wide intervals can cover many outcomes without being useful. Calibration needs enough independent observations and an explicit evaluation window.
after: A forecast range needs a separate test. How often did it contain the outcome, and how wide was it? A wide range can contain many outcomes while telling you little. Testing whether ranges match their stated confidence level needs enough independent observations over a clearly defined period.
note: Retains error definition, sample limit, coverage versus width and calibration requirements; explains calibration rather than leaving jargon unexplained.

before: What this example establishes
after: What the worked example can show

before: Blocks arrive irregularly. Projecting from the pace so far assumes something about the rest of the adjustment period; it does not measure a future network value. Calendar timing is also an estimate.
after: Blocks do not arrive at regular intervals. Extending the pace so far into the rest of the adjustment period requires an assumption about future block timing. It does not measure a future network value. The estimated calendar date can change too.

To repeat the calculation, sort its 26 adjustment blocks by height and check that consecutive blocks are 2,016 blocks apart. Exclude the earliest: its preceding difficulty is outside the snapshot. For each remaining adjustment, calculate 100 × (new difficulty / previous difficulty − 1). Do not use the provider’s rounded adjustment ratio.

The citation manifest lists SHA-256 digests, which are file checksums, for the original response and CSV/JSON downloads. These let readers detect changes from this version.

after: All findings and downloads are available without email. Version 1.0.0 has a stable dataset identifier and a citation manifest. note: Names the effect being examined rather than telling a reviewer what to compare (habit 1).

after: Changing the difficulty path changes the production and payback estimates for a fleet. To see the effect of that assumption, compare several paths while keeping power cost, uptime, capital cost and Bitcoin price constant. Otherwise, a difference in the result may come from another input.
note: Preserves fleet comparison, production/payback, all four other inputs and the reason for holding them constant. No new number, financial example or measured result (habits 1, 3).

before: Keep the decision proportional to the evidence
after: What a calculator cannot decide

This article provides no measured threshold at which an operation should hedge.

That also depends on timing, transaction costs, available liquidity and operational constraints. This article provides no measured threshold at which an operation should hedge.

before: An estimate from observable inputs
after: How network hashrate is estimated

before: Compare like with like
after: Why two charts can differ
note: Names the question answered by this section (E31).

after: Blocks arrive irregularly, so estimates over short and long windows can differ. Comparing two charts also requires matching timestamps and difficulty inputs. A change on a chart alone does not establish that mining capacity has changed.
note: Preserves irregular arrival, window differences, timestamp/difficulty matching and the limit on inferring capacity. No claim about a particular observed movement (habit 3).

before: Ask how uncertainty was estimated
after: What an error band can tell you

note: Explains why construction and assumptions matter; preserves both explicit limits on measured width and attribution of recent movement to noise. No performance claim (habits 3, 4).

before: Difficulty sets the work needed to find a valid block. How it adjusts, what it does to expected BTC production and why its timing is an estimate.
after: Difficulty sets the work needed to find a valid block. Adjustments affect expected BTC production; the next adjustment’s date remains an estimate.
note: Turns the fragment into connected explanation. Definition and production/timing distinctions preserved (habit 3). Parent review: tightened the card/metadata summary; supporting detail and all qualifications remain in the article.

before: Bitcoin adjusts mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to target an average block interval of about ten minutes. Each adjustment uses the elapsed time of the preceding period: faster block production raises difficulty and slower production lowers it, within the protocol’s limits.
after: Bitcoin adjusts mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to target an average block interval of about ten minutes. The adjustment uses the time taken by the preceding period. Faster block production raises difficulty and slower production lowers it, within the protocol’s limits.
note: Splits the long second sentence. Keeps every numeric fact, averaging qualifier, preceding-period basis, directions and protocol limits. No new mechanism (habit 3, E29).

before: Individual blocks arrive irregularly. A target block height is specific, but the calendar date when it will arrive is estimated. A difficulty forecast projects the adjustment before the observation is complete.
after: Individual blocks arrive irregularly, so a specified block height does not give an exact calendar date. A difficulty forecast estimates the next adjustment before all the blocks in the observation period have arrived.
note: Connects irregular blocks to estimated calendar timing and explains the incomplete observation period. Preserves specific height versus estimated date and forecast status (habit 3).

before: Read expected mining revenue per unit of hashrate and time, with the denomination and assumptions visible.
after: Hashprice measures expected mining revenue per unit of hashrate and time. Its currency, units and calculation assumptions matter when comparing figures.
note: Replaces a review instruction with what hashprice describes and why comparisons require care. Keeps expected revenue, time, hashrate, denomination and assumptions (habit 3).

before: Hashprice expresses mining revenue per unit of hashrate over a stated time period. It can be denominated in Bitcoin or converted into a currency such as US dollars. Always check those units before comparing figures.
after: Hashprice expresses mining revenue per unit of hashrate over a stated time period. It can be denominated in Bitcoin or converted into a currency such as US dollars. A comparison needs the same currency, hashrate units and time period.
note: Keeps the natural definition and denomination examples. Makes the units check specific using the dimensions already stated, without adding example values (habit 3).

before: Check the inputs
after: Why published hashprices can differ

after: Hashprice depends on difficulty, block rewards and transaction fees. When it is expressed in a currency such as US dollars, the Bitcoin price source also matters. Publishers can report different values if they use different observation periods, averaging methods or price timestamps.
note: Preserves every calculation input and source of methodological difference, without attributing a real publisher discrepancy to any cause (habit 3).

after: Hashprice does not measure profit
note: Makes the economic distinction explicit rather than instructing a reviewer to preserve it (habit 4).

after: Hashprice describes revenue, not an operation’s margin. Profit also depends on power, hosting, maintenance and other costs, as well as fleet efficiency and uptime. Revenue and costs need to be expressed in compatible units for the comparison to be meaningful.

after: A forecast range needs an explanation of how it was calculated, which assumptions it uses and how often it is intended to contain the outcome. A range derived from a theoretical model and one fitted to observed data both need evaluation. The label alone does not show that either works.

note: Matches the current calculator control without changing its values or behaviour.

after: Starting difficulty

after: Choose a constant Bitcoin price and enter a monthly Difficulty growth guess. The default 1.5% is an illustrative input, not a site forecast.

before: Compare the central row with the lower-growth and higher-growth rows. Lower growth is the selected rate minus two percentage points, floored at zero; higher growth is the selected rate plus three points.

before: Check the final cumulative cash balance alongside the payback month.

before: Copy the URL to retain inputs. Share only assumptions you are comfortable exposing.

note: Uses exact current control labels, explains how to read results and preserves units, offsets, floors, defaults, URL inputs and privacy (habits 3, 5).

before: Assumed difficulty growth

after: Check a block-data source you trust and enter its value in Starting difficulty.

after: The first month when mining revenue, after power costs, has recovered the initial outlay in the central scenario.

before: Cash after the modeled horizon
after: Cash after the modelled horizon

before: Reproduce the example: a static assumption versus a range

before: Compare an advertised hosting rate with fees and paid lost hours. Check billing assumptions before comparing quotes.
after: Compare a hosting rate with fees and hours you pay for while machines are stopped. Use the same billing assumptions for each quote.

before: A normalised cost comparison for hosting priced per kWh. It adds management and power-factor percentages to the advertised rate, divides by the share of productive hours, and divides by one minus the pool-fee fraction. The result is an equivalent cost per productive kWh, not an actual invoice or a profit calculation.
after: This calculator compares hosting costs per productive kWh. It adds management and power-factor percentages to the advertised rate, then divides by the share of hours when machines run. It then divides by one minus the pool-fee fraction. The result is an equivalent cost for comparison, not an actual invoice or profit calculation.
note: Explains the three operations in sequence. Preserves the additive fees, productive-hours divisor and pool divisor exactly (habits 3, 5).

before: For machine owners comparing hosting terms when booked power capacity remains payable during lost hours. A business that hosts other people’s machines may also use it for machines it owns. Energy-only billing, revenue-share contracts, demand-response income and unrelated hosting income require different models.
after: Use this if you own machines and pay for booked hosting capacity even when the machines are stopped. Hosting businesses can use it for machines they own. Energy-only billing, revenue-share contracts, demand-response income and unrelated hosting income need different models.
note: Replaces booked-capacity/lost-hours nesting with a concrete billing condition. Keeps every excluded model.

before: Check your agreement and invoices. Confirm which fees are already included in the advertised rate and whether lost hours remain payable.
after: Check the agreement and invoices. Which fees are included in the advertised rate, and do you still pay when machines stop?
note: Makes billing checks and input sources easy to follow. Keeps percentage bases, non-overlap, pool-equivalent and privacy limits (habit 5).

before: Enter the advertised rate in $/kWh. Enter management and power-factor adjustments as percentages of that rate; do not enter a fee twice.
after: Enter Advertised power rate in $/kWh. Enter management and power-factor fees as percentages of that rate. Do not add a fee already included in the rate.
note: Makes billing checks and input sources easy to follow. Keeps percentage bases, non-overlap, pool-equivalent and privacy limits (habit 5).

before: Enter distinct downtime and curtailment hours as percentages of the same period. Do not count an hour in both. Use actual records or explicitly labelled assumptions.
after: Enter downtime and curtailment as percentages of the same period. Use records or clearly labelled assumptions. Count each stopped hour once, under one input only.
note: Makes billing checks and input sources easy to follow. Keeps percentage bases, non-overlap, pool-equivalent and privacy limits (habit 5).

before: Enter the pool-fee percentage. The tool converts it to an equivalent cost adjustment; a pool’s charge on revenue is not an electricity charge.
after: Enter Pool fee as a percentage of revenue. The tool converts it to an equivalent cost for comparison; it is not an electricity charge.
note: Makes billing checks and input sources easy to follow. Keeps percentage bases, non-overlap, pool-equivalent and privacy limits (habit 5).

before: Compare all steps and the absolute final rates for two offers under consistent assumptions. A small percentage uplift can still produce a higher absolute cost.
after: Compare each step and the final rates using the same assumptions for both offers. A smaller percentage increase can still leave you with a higher final cost.
note: Makes billing checks and input sources easy to follow. Keeps percentage bases, non-overlap, pool-equivalent and privacy limits (habit 5).

before: Copy the URL to retain the inputs. Anyone with that URL can read the terms you entered.
after: Copy the URL to save the inputs. Anyone with the link can read the terms you entered.
note: Makes billing checks and input sources easy to follow. Keeps percentage bases, non-overlap, pool-equivalent and privacy limits (habit 5).

before: Billing terms or a measured charge from your host. A technical power-factor specification alone may not describe your invoice.
after: Use the billing terms or a charge on your host’s invoice. A machine’s power-factor specification alone may not match what you are billed.
note: Names an actionable source and preserves the distinction between technical specification and invoice.

before: A share of the same measured period when machines were unavailable and booked capacity remained payable.
after: The percentage of the period when machines were unexpectedly unavailable but you still paid for booked capacity.
note: Explains downtime as an actual billing condition, preserving period, availability and paid capacity.

before: Pool or site records reconciled with billing.
after: Compare pool or site records with the invoices for the same period.
note: Explains reconciled-with-billing as the actual task.

before: A separate share of deliberately stopped hours for which booked capacity remains payable.
after: The percentage of hours when machines were deliberately stopped but booked capacity was still payable. Count these separately from unplanned downtime.
note: Explains curtailment and retains the non-overlap requirement.

before: A revenue percentage represented here as an equivalent cost adjustment.
after: The percentage of revenue paid to the pool, converted here to an equivalent cost for comparison.
note: Names who receives the fee and why it appears in a cost model.

before: Compare absolute values under matching billing assumptions. This is not an invoice, revenue or profit.
after: Compare final costs using the same billing assumptions. The result is an equivalent cost, not an invoice, revenue or profit.
note: Makes absolute-values-under-matching-assumptions concrete; keeps the financial boundaries.

before: This measures the effect of entered assumptions. It cannot establish a provider’s honesty or quality.
after: This shows how your inputs change the starting rate. It does not rate the provider’s honesty or quality.
note: Explains the uplift measure without implying a provider assessment.

before: Separate steps show which inputs contribute to the final equivalent cost. Pool-fee adjustment follows those steps.
after: The rows show how fees and paid lost hours change the rate. The pool-fee adjustment comes after these steps.
note: Connects result rows to the calculation order; no formula change.

before: The result follows the entered billing and lost-hours assumptions. Comparing another offer requires the same treatment of tax, fees and paid lost hours.
after: The result depends on the billing terms and paid lost hours you entered. To compare another offer, treat tax, fees and paid lost hours in the same way.
note: Connects result to the inputs and gives the comparison task directly.

before: An order, a position and a payout are different
after: Orders, positions and payouts
note: Shortens the heading while keeping the three distinct stages.

before: An order is an instruction to buy or sell. If it fills, you hold shares: the position tokens for one side of the market. Execution depends on available liquidity, so a market or limit order may not fill in full.
after: An order is an instruction to buy or sell. A filled buy adds shares to your holding; a filled sell reduces it. Shares are the position tokens for one side of the market. Execution depends on available liquidity, so a market or limit order may not fill in full.
note: Explains the order-to-holding relationship for both buys and sells. Retains the definition of shares and incomplete-execution warning; Managing positions already specifies that filled sells reduce shares.

before: Start with mining difficulty and market mechanics if the underlying is new to you. Read settlement and the risks before moving to the app guides.
after: If mining difficulty is new to you, start with the mining difficulty and market mechanics guides. Read about settlement and risks before moving to the app guides.
note: Replaces “the underlying” with the subject the reader needs to understand; retains the reading order and warning before app use.

before: The app guides cover signing in, funding, orders and account actions. Reference pages explain the terms and the evidence to check. Use the optional calculators to explore your own assumptions.
after: The app guides cover signing in, funding, orders and account actions. Reference pages explain terms, collateral, contract audits and forecasting methods. Use the optional calculators to explore your own assumptions.
note: Names the subjects covered by the reference pages instead of asking readers to “check evidence”. Retains the app-guide categories and assumption-based optional calculators.

before: Bitcoin periodically adjusts difficulty using elapsed time in the preceding adjustment period. Faster block production generally leads to higher difficulty, and slower production generally leads to lower difficulty, subject to the protocol’s rules.
after: Bitcoin adjusts difficulty based on how long the preceding adjustment period took. Faster block production generally leads to higher difficulty, and slower production generally leads to lower difficulty, subject to the protocol’s rules.
note: Explains elapsed time in familiar words. Retains both directions and the protocol qualification.

before: Production and revenue are broader questions
after: Difficulty, production and revenue
note: Names the section’s subjects directly; the production and revenue qualifications stay intact.

before: Separate the market outcome from your operation
after: The limits of a difficulty position
note: Replaces an abstract instruction with the limit the section explains.

before: Read price relative to the full payout
after: How price implies a probability
note: Names the calculation explained immediately below.

before: Separate the display from an executable quote
after: Displayed prices and available trades
note: Distinguishes price displays from executable trades without the long noun phrase.

before: Review the available depth and your order preview. A wide spread or thin order book can make the displayed probability a weak summary of what participants would actually trade.
after: Check the available depth and your order preview. When the spread is wide or the order book is thin, the displayed probability may tell you little about the prices and quantities participants will trade.
note: Explains why depth matters in terms of actual prices and quantities; retains the wide-spread and thin-book qualifications.

before: Keep the outcome and cost basis separate
after: Payout and profit
note: Names the distinction already explained by the existing paragraph; adds no payout claim or example.

before: Check the current market specification, transaction confirmation, applicable terms and access requirements. An organisation should also resolve its internal permissions and review requirements. Contact the team for current information when the documents or app do not answer a material question.
after: Before funding, read the current market specification, transaction confirmation, applicable terms and access requirements. If you act for an organisation, confirm its internal permissions and review requirements too. Ask the team about any material question the documents or app leave unanswered.
note: Keeps the funding checkpoint, all four external checks, organisational permissions and review, and the escalation route. Makes the instruction personal and direct.

before: If account setup is required, the app presents it before the order. Read that confirmation and any signing request. Then review the order confirmation itself; setup completion is not an order fill.
after: If account setup is required, the app presents it before the order. Read that confirmation and any signing request, then review the order confirmation. Completing setup does not mean the order has filled.
note: Replaces “setup completion is not an order fill” with a natural sentence. Retains conditional setup, signing request and separate order confirmation.

before: After submission, inspect the order status and filled amount in Portfolio. An accepted or open order is not the same as a completed trade. Reconcile any remaining open amount before placing a replacement, and use the resulting position balance to confirm the exposure you hold.
after: After submitting, open Portfolio and check the order status and filled amount. An accepted or open order is not the same as a completed trade. Check how much remains open before placing a replacement, then use your position balance to see the exposure you hold.
note: Turns “reconcile” and “resulting position balance” into concrete checks. Keeps accepted/open versus completed, remaining amount before replacement and the actual holding.

before: Review the actual quote, available amount and any partial-fill warning. An empty or changing book can prevent execution. Refresh the quote when the app requires it rather than treating an earlier preview as a guarantee.
after: Review the current quote, available amount and any partial-fill warning. An empty or changing book can prevent execution. Refresh the quote when the app requires it; an earlier preview does not guarantee execution.
note: States what to do and why without the “rather than treating” construction. Keeps amount, partial fills, changing liquidity and required refresh.

before: Cancellation and replacement can fail separately. If cancellation succeeded but the replacement was not signed or accepted, the old order is cancelled and there may be no replacement. Check Orders before submitting again.
after: Cancellation and replacement are separate steps and either can fail. If cancellation succeeds but the replacement is not signed or accepted, the old order is cancelled and there may be no replacement. Check Orders before submitting again.
note: Explains the two possible failures in a connected sequence. Retains unsigned/unaccepted replacement and the check before retrying.

before: Reconcile reserved funds
after: Check reserved funds
note: Uses the action the reader can take instead of “reconcile”.

before: After a change, check Total, Locked and Available balances. A pending action or an old balance does not confirm that funds have been released. If you ask the team to investigate, include the latest order status and any transaction or request reference.
after: After a change, check Total, Locked and Available balances. Funds may still be reserved while an action is pending or the displayed balance is out of date. If you ask the team to investigate, include the latest order status and any transaction or request reference.
note: Explains why a pending action or old balance cannot confirm released funds. Keeps all balance labels and the support references.

before: Losing shares have no payout. Redemption proceeds are gross: your result is the amount redeemed minus what you paid and any costs.
after: Losing shares have no payout. To work out your profit or loss, subtract what you paid and any costs from the amount redeemed.
note: Explains gross proceeds with the calculation itself. Retains zero payout for losing shares and the same amount-redeemed minus cost calculation; no figures or returns added.

before: Wait for the confirmed result. A transaction reference or “submitted” message does not yet establish that the recipient has received the funds.
after: A transaction reference or a “submitted” message does not confirm that the recipient has received the funds. Wait for the confirmed result.
note: Puts the warning before the wait and replaces “establish” with “confirm”. Keeps the submitted-versus-received distinction.

before: The token is part of the market specification
after: Check the market’s collateral token
note: Gives the task directly; the section retains market-specific funding and payout, token list and token risks.

before: The app may ask you to set up your account or approve a token before continuing. Read what the current confirmation allows. An earlier approval for one token does not establish support for another token or contract.
after: The app may ask you to set up your account or approve a token before continuing. Read the confirmation to see what you are authorising. An earlier approval for one token does not establish support for another token or contract.
note: Makes the purpose of reading a confirmation explicit. Retains conditional setup/approval and the limit on what an earlier approval establishes.

before: Separate account, order and token operations
after: Signatures and contract transactions
note: Names the distinction explained below, without an abstract imperative.

before: Request the audit reports, commit or version reviewed, scope, outstanding findings and remediation evidence.
after: Ask for audit reports, including the commit or version reviewed, the scope, unresolved findings and evidence of fixes.
note: Replaces compressed review jargon with a concrete request. Keeps version, scope, outstanding findings and remediation evidence.

before: Review account permissions, token approvals, resolution dependencies and the operational process for interruptions.
after: Check account permissions, token approvals, dependencies involved in resolution and the process for handling interruptions.
note: Unpacks “resolution dependencies” and “operational process” while preserving all four review areas.

before: Any uncertainty range needs a construction method and evaluation against outcomes. Compare interval coverage and width across a stated evaluation window; a range alone does not establish calibration.
after: To judge an uncertainty range, you need to know how it was calculated and how it performed against actual outcomes. Over a stated evaluation window, compare how often outcomes fell within the range and how wide it was. A range alone does not show that it is calibrated.
note: Explains construction method, interval coverage and width in ordinary language. Keeps the evaluation window and the warning that a range alone does not establish calibration.

before: Because publishers compute it differently. The differences sit almost entirely in the price leg: which exchanges are in the basket, how they are weighted and when the snapshot is taken. Few publishers disclose the basket.
after: Because publishers calculate it differently. Most differences come from the Bitcoin price used: which exchanges are included, how they are weighted and when the price is recorded. Few publishers disclose which exchanges they use.
note: Explains 'the price leg' and the exchange 'basket' in plain words. Preserves the exchange selection, weighting, snapshot timing and limited disclosure; E30 names the method instead of using an image.

before: Because behaviour before and after a halving differs so much that models spanning the boundary tend to mislead. A fit window should state which side of a halving it sits on.
after: Because behaviour before and after a halving differs so much that models spanning the boundary tend to mislead. A model should state whether the period used to fit it is before or after a halving.
note: Replaces 'fit window' and 'which side ... it sits on' with the period used to fit the model. Retains the warning about models spanning a halving; precision before punch, habit 3.

before: Because terahash is the unit in which a fleet's revenue is most easily reasoned about. It is also the scale of an individual machine.
after: Because it is the easiest unit to use when working out a fleet's revenue. It is also the scale of an individual machine.
note: Replaces the passive abstraction 'the unit in which ... most easily reasoned about' with a direct explanation. Retains the fleet revenue and individual-machine scales; plain register, habit 10.

before: Luck dominates short-run pool comparisons. A payout comparison between pools needs the variance maths shown alongside it; without it, a difference that is pure chance reads as a better pool.
after: Luck dominates short-run pool comparisons. A comparison of pool payouts needs to show how much they can vary by chance. Without that, a difference caused purely by luck can make one pool look better.
note: Explains 'the variance maths' and resolves the awkward 'reads as a better pool'. Preserves the need to show chance variation alongside comparisons; E30 uses a concrete explanation.

before: Difficulty stays fixed for a whole epoch and changes only at its boundary. That makes the epoch the natural unit of time for anyone managing difficulty exposure: production, forecasts and settlement all align to epoch boundaries rather than to calendar dates.
after: Difficulty stays fixed during an epoch and changes at its boundary. Epochs are useful when comparing production and difficulty forecasts. Each Doefin market specifies the block at which difficulty is observed. Check the market’s terms for its observation and settlement blocks.
note: Parent and independent review: Factual clarity: removes the unsupported claim that all production, forecasts and settlement align to epoch boundaries. Uses the existing market-specific observation/settlement distinction; does not claim arbitrary non-boundary block support. Requires Matteo reading before publication.

before: A band derived from theory rather than from measured forecast error is typically two to three times too narrow. The first comparison with real outcomes shows the gap.
after: A range calculated from theory and one fitted to historical data both need testing against outcomes. Compare how often the ranges contain the outcome with their stated confidence level.
note: Parent and independent review: Factual clarity: removes the unsupported universal two-to-three-times claim. Consistent with the published Academy and methodology requirement to evaluate theoretical and fitted intervals. Requires Matteo reading before publication.

before: Why are theoretical confidence intervals usually too narrow?
after: How do you check a forecast range?
note: Parent and independent review: Factual clarity: removes the presupposition that theoretical ranges are usually too narrow; asks the reader’s actual evaluation question. Requires Matteo reading before publication.

before: Because they are derived from theory rather than fitted to measured forecast error. An interval only means something once it has been fitted to what actually happened.
after: Compare the published ranges with the outcomes over a stated evaluation period. Report how often the ranges contained the outcome alongside their widths. Fitting a range to past data does not by itself show how it will perform on new forecasts.
note: Parent and independent review: Factual clarity: neither theory nor empirical fitting validates an interval by itself. Retains the need for recorded outcomes and explains coverage and width without introducing figures. Requires Matteo reading before publication.

before: A one-day estimate carries an uncertainty band of roughly ±16%. Over seven days the band narrows to about ±6%, so a one-day move is usually noise rather than a trend.
after: Short observation windows can fluctuate because blocks arrive irregularly. A chart alone does not establish that mining capacity has changed. Check the publisher’s calculation, time window, timestamp and uncertainty range.
note: Parent and independent review: Factual clarity: removes context-free ±16% and ±6% claims and the unsupported conclusion that a one-day move is usually noise. The existing article explains irregular blocks and the need to compare method, window and uncertainty. Requires Matteo reading before publication.

before: Hashprice falls when difficulty rises, when the Bitcoin price falls or when transaction fees fall. A 10% rise in difficulty, for example, cuts hashprice by about 9.1%, all else equal.
after: Hashprice falls when difficulty rises or transaction fees fall, all else equal. When quoted in US dollars, it also falls when the Bitcoin price falls. For example, a 10% rise in difficulty cuts hashprice by about 9.1%, all else equal.
note: Parent and independent review: Factual clarity: limits the BTC-price effect to USD-denominated hashprice, consistent with its unchanged approved short definition. Preserves the 10%/about9.1% example and its all-else-equal condition. Requires Matteo reading before publication.
